terms.definition: Clusters of sensory-neuron cell bodies beside the spinal cord. Each neuron sends one branch to the body (skin, gut, organs) and another into the spinal cord.
The shape of a DRG sensory neuron: a single process leaves the cell body and splits — one branch to the periphery, one to the spinal cord.
The sensory-input region of the spinal cord's grey matter, where DRG afferents terminate and are sorted by type.
A sensory neuron that detects noxious (potentially harmful) stimuli and can signal pain.
Low-threshold mechanoreceptor — a sensory neuron that fires to light mechanical force.
High-threshold mechanoreceptor — a sensory neuron that fires only to strong mechanical force, as in painful distension.
A mechanically gated ion channel that opens when the membrane is stretched; key for touch and for sensing gut and visceral distension.
A sensory ion channel activated by heat and capsaicin; marks many nociceptors and is often used to target them.
The gut's own intrinsic network of neurons in the bowel wall, controlling motility and secretion and interacting with extrinsic afferents.
A recombinase enzyme that cuts DNA at loxP sites. Driven from a cell-type promoter, it switches on a floxed payload only in those cells.
A 34-bp DNA tag that Cre recognizes. DNA flanked by two loxP sites is 'floxed'; Cre excises or inverts the sequence between them.
A version of Cre held inactive in the cytoplasm until the drug tamoxifen is given, so recombination happens only when (and where) you choose.
A drug that lets CreER enter the nucleus and recombine DNA. Dose sets how many cells are labeled — low dose gives sparse, single-cell labeling.
A second recombinase, independent of Cre, that acts at FRT sites. Using Cre and Flp together lets you require two conditions at once.
The DNA site the Flp recombinase recognizes — the Flp equivalent of loxP.
Targeting only cells that meet two criteria at once (e.g. Cre AND Flp), to isolate a population no single marker captures cleanly.
A payload such as a fluorophore (tdTomato, GFP) switched on by Cre to mark and visualize specific cells.
Designer Receptor Exclusively Activated by a Designer Drug — an engineered GPCR that ignores its natural ligand and responds only to an otherwise-inert drug, letting you turn neurons up or down.
An excitatory DREADD. It couples to Gq and drives a neuron toward firing when the actuator is given.
An inhibitory DREADD. It couples to Gi/o and silences a neuron when the actuator is given.
G-protein-coupled receptor — a membrane receptor that signals through intracellular G proteins. DREADDs are engineered GPCRs.
Controlling specific cells with an engineered receptor plus a designer drug (e.g. DREADDs), giving slow, minutes-scale control of activity.
The original DREADD actuator. Once assumed inert, it is partly back-converted to clozapine, which has its own effects.
An antipsychotic with many receptor targets. CNO converts to it in the body, so it can cause effects not due to the DREADD.
A newer DREADD actuator, more potent and selective than CNO and effective at much lower doses.
The drug that activates a DREADD (CNO or DCZ). It is given systemically but only affects cells expressing the DREADD.
An immediate-early gene whose protein rises in recently active neurons, used to confirm that a manipulation actually drove firing.
Adeno-associated virus — the standard non-pathogenic vector for delivering a payload (reporter, sensor, DREADD) to chosen cells by injection.
The capsid (outer-shell) variant of an AAV, which sets which cells it enters and whether it travels along axons.
Which cell types a virus efficiently infects, determined largely by its serotype.
Transport from axon terminals back toward the cell body. A retrograde AAV injected in an organ labels the neurons that project there.
A Cre-dependent viral design (also called FLEX): the payload is inverted until Cre flips it on, so it expresses only in Cre+ cells.
A comparison condition that holds everything constant except the one thing you're testing, so a result means a difference between conditions.
A sample known to give a signal. If it fails, the assay itself didn't work — it rules out false negatives.
A condition that should give no signal. If it does, something is non-specific — it rules out false positives.
The drug's carrier solution given without the active compound, to separate the compound's effect from the delivery.
An independent biological sample (e.g. a different animal); captures real variation between subjects and sets your n for biological claims.
A repeated measurement of the same sample (e.g. triplicate qPCR wells); captures measurement noise, not biological variation.
Keeping the experimenter or scorer unaware of group identity so expectation can't bias the result.
The probability of seeing an effect at least this large if there were truly no effect. A small p doesn't mean the effect is large, real, or reproducible.
The central nervous system — the brain and spinal cord, where signals are integrated.
The peripheral nervous system — the nerves and ganglia outside the brain and spinal cord that connect them to the body.
Carrying information toward the CNS; sensory neurons are afferent ('A' for arriving).
Carrying commands away from the CNS to muscles or glands; motor/output neurons are efferent ('E' for exiting).
The division handling voluntary skeletal-muscle control and sensation from skin, muscle and joints.
The division running involuntary interior functions — smooth muscle, glands and the heart — through motor (efferent) output.
The autonomic branch that mobilizes the body ('fight or flight'); thoracolumbar outflow.
The autonomic branch that supports rest and digestion; craniosacral outflow, including the vagus nerve.
A cluster of neuronal cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system (the CNS equivalent is a nucleus).
An autonomic neuron running from the CNS to a peripheral ganglion, where it synapses.
An autonomic neuron running from a ganglion to the target organ.
A mixed nerve leaving each spinal segment, formed where the dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots join.
The sensory entry into the spinal cord; it carries DRG afferent axons and bears the DRG.
The motor exit from the spinal cord, carrying efferent axons to muscles and autonomic targets.
The strip of skin whose sensation is carried by a single spinal segment.
The ganglion holding the cell bodies of vagal sensory neurons — the vagal counterpart of the DRG.
The major parasympathetic nerve; its sensory (nodose) branch carries much interoceptive information from internal organs.
The first part of the small intestine, just after the stomach; bile and pancreatic juice empty into it.
The innermost layer of the gut wall: the lining epithelium, the lamina propria beneath it, and a thin muscle sheet.
Connective tissue just under the gut epithelium, rich in immune cells and sensory nerve endings.
The gut-wall layer under the mucosa, with blood vessels and the submucosal plexus.
The gut's main muscle coat: an inner circular and outer longitudinal layer, with the myenteric plexus between them.
The enteric nerve network between the gut's two muscle layers; it mainly controls motility.
The enteric nerve network in the submucosa; it mainly controls secretion and local blood flow.
Secreting into a duct or onto a surface rather than into the blood. Most of the pancreas is exocrine.
Secreting hormones directly into the blood. The pancreatic islets are the endocrine part of the pancreas.
A pancreatic exocrine cell, clustered in grape-like acini, that makes digestive enzymes.
An inactive enzyme precursor (such as trypsinogen) that is switched on only after it leaves the cell, so the pancreas doesn't digest itself.
A small cluster of endocrine cells in the pancreas that releases insulin, glucagon and other hormones into the blood.
The islet cell that makes insulin.
The islet cell that makes glucagon.
A duodenal hormone released by acid; it tells pancreatic duct cells to secrete bicarbonate.
A duodenal hormone released by fats and proteins; it drives pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.
A sympathetic (prevertebral) ganglion near the celiac artery that sends postganglionic fibers to upper abdominal organs, including the pancreas.
Nerves linking the thoracic/lumbar spinal cord to abdominal organs; they carry sympathetic preganglionic fibers out and spinal (DRG) sensory fibers back.
